s21.music: The St. Brendan’s Choir — “Soon and Very Soon”
body: The nine o’clock is the candle Mass. St. Brendan’s is lit from the floor up — tapers on every sill under the blue glass, gone black now; the sanctuary lamp; the votive rack at the shrine like a town seen from a hill at night — and over all of it the fir ribs go up into the dark like the hull of a boat somebody turned over and left. The student choir has two guitars and Kenzie Rourke on tambourine, and they take the processional at a clip, *soon and very soon*, like they intend to have everybody before the King by ten.
Becca has saved three seats in the fourth pew on the left, her coat on one and her planner on the other. She moves the planner for Jack and leaves the coat. “For Lena,” she whispers.

Lena comes up the side aisle during the second verse with the black mantilla over her hair, and Julian Park-Ellis is a step behind her in a cardigan mended at both elbows. He isn’t carrying anything, and his right hand keeps closing on a guitar-case handle that isn’t there.

Becca lights up, and there’s nothing in it but welcome. “Oh! *Scoot*.” She scoots; Jack scoots; Lena slides in on his right with Julian on the aisle. Becca, Jack, Lena, Julian. “Julian,” Lena murmurs across him, and that’s the introduction. “She brought *somebody*,” Becca whispers into Jack’s shoulder, and squeezes his arm about it, and finds the page.

Julian has never sat through a Mass, and it shows the way a new guy shows on a loading dock: he stands half a second after everybody and sits half a second after, and watches Lena’s hands to find out what to do with his. He doesn’t try the responses. He listens to them.

Father Osei reads the Gospel himself — the sun darkened, the stars falling out of the sky — and then, without changing his voice, the fig tree. *Learn a lesson from the fig tree. When its branch becomes tender and sprouts leaves, you know that summer is near.* On Jack’s right Lena stops moving. Not her hands, not her breath; the lace at her temple doesn’t stir.

body.text: Jack thinks of a shotgun house on Zimple Street he has never seen: For Sale since the storm, a fig in the side yard, and on the back porch, under the fig, a claw-foot tub.
body.else: Jack thinks of a shotgun house on Zimple Street he has never seen: For Sale since the storm, a fig in the side yard.

body: The homily is short, even for Osei. “Heaven and earth will pass away,” he says, and waits out a cough in the back. “He doesn’t say *you* will. He says His words won’t.” He sits down, and the choir has to scramble.

At the consecration Jack kneels between Becca and Lena, a shoulder on either side of him, and for as long as the bells go he isn’t thinking about anybody at all. Julian kneels when the pew kneels and then stays down through the Our Father, alone on the kneeler with the church standing over him, until Lena touches his sleeve. At Communion he lets them by and sits back down by himself with his hands folded, and watches her go up.

In the crush at the doors afterward, with the choir still going, Jack hears him under his breath, humming the second Hosanna — the Holy, Holy he didn’t know an hour ago — and getting every note of it right.

journal.title: Julian Park-Ellis
journal.text: Julian Park-Ellis. The guitar guy from the Lighthouse stairs. Plays Bastille Thursdays. Wrote a song called “Fresno.” Plays it once a month. All Souls: came to St. Brendan’s to write Nora Calloway’s name in the book. She was his friend. They sang together. He saw us leave in the second chorus. Something new Thursday. A handshake you’d trust with anything. Sunday he came to the nine o’clock with Lena. Didn’t receive. Had the Sanctus by ear by the end.

s22.slug: SUNDAY · 10:05 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE COURTYARD WALL
body: Afterward the courtyard is fifty-five degrees and perfectly still. The olive doesn’t stir. There’s no moon, and over the roof of the Newman house there are more stars than Marisol usually admits to, and low in the south one of them isn’t twinkling at all — just sitting there, brighter than everything else, steady as a porch light. Jupiter. Planets don’t twinkle. Jack learned that in the fourth grade and has been waiting nine years for it to come up.

Becca was across Ocean Road to the Ranger by two minutes past ten — the lab at eight. She hugged Jack hard, and then Lena, and then, after a second, Julian, who held still for it like he’d been warned and then hugged her back.

“I’ll get us coffees,” Julian says. He’s already turning toward the yellow door of the Newman house when he sees Jack on the wall, and the turn slows. “Take your time,” he tells Lena, and crosses the flagstones toward the light.
Lena sits up on the low wall with the mantilla folded in her lap and her boots hanging, and Jack sits beside her. It’s a week to the night. He said he’d ask, and he asks.
“So,” he says. “The table.”
He means the table, and only the table.

body.text: The joke he almost made on the walk to Lupe’s — *come to Youngstown, nobody there’s ever heard his name* — is still in his pocket, and it’s a different *his* now.

body: She has an answer ready; she’s had a week to get it ready. “I’ll be okay at that table,” she says. “Wes will sit where he sits, and Josie will bite somebody, and Daddy will carve.” She breathes in through her nose and lets it go. “Julian says call him from the bathroom if I need to.”
It’s good advice. It’s exactly right, and Jack, who also had a week, didn’t think of it.
“You were nice about Friday,” Lena says.
“I’m nice.”
“You’re not, usually.” She knocks her boot heel against his. “That’s how I knew you meant it.”

Then she wants to hear about his, and he gives her the Greyhound like it’s a pilgrimage. Two and a half days. Changes in Denver and Chicago. He’s packing a rosary, a paperback and a sandwich he means to ration like the Donner Party, and by the law of averages he’ll be seated next to a man who sells knives out of a sample case and has a position on the moon landing. She’s still laughing at the knives when he gets to Nebraska, which he understands is four hundred miles of one cow standing in different places, and he does the cow. Lena has to hold on to the wall.
“You’re going to come home a prophet,” she says, “or a serial killer.”
“In Youngstown they’ll want to know which before they set a place.”

Julian comes back across the flagstones with two coffees in Newman mugs, the white ones with the little leather boat on the side, and does the arithmetic — three people, two mugs — without breaking stride. He holds his out. “Jack. Take it. I’ll get another.”

choices.text: Take it.
response: Jack takes it. The mug is hot right through, too hot to hold properly, and he wraps his hands around it anyway and lets it burn a little.

Julian goes back in for another and comes out with it, and the three of them drink their coffee on the wall till the mugs are cold, talking about the fig tree and whether Osei times his homilies with a watch. Then they go out the gate to Ocean Road together, Julian on the street side.

choices.text: “I’m good.”
response: “I’m good,” Jack says.

Julian doesn’t argue, and he doesn’t look put out. He sits down on Lena’s other side, and the two of them pass the one mug back and forth for the rest of it without either of them seeming to notice they’re doing it. When it’s empty the three of them go out the gate to Ocean Road together.

choices.text: “You cut the second chorus.”
response: “You cut the second chorus,” Jack says, and leaves the mug where it is.

Julian glances past him at Lena on the wall, and something in his face goes very gentle. “Somebody had to stay to the end,” he says. He sits down on her other side and gives her hers and keeps his, and when the mugs are empty the three of them go out the gate to Ocean Road together.

journal.title: Thanksgiving
journal.text: Wes will be at the Broussards’ table on Thanksgiving, like every year since the storm. He carried the twins out of a second floor. Lena says she’d go anywhere nobody knows his name. I’m going to ask her to Youngstown — properly, in a week. Not one breath after Becca’s name. A week to the night, I asked about the table. She’ll be okay. Julian says call him from the bathroom. I didn’t ask the other thing.

body: Monday Night Football with nothing riding on it sounds like a pool game nobody’s winning and the ice machine dumping a load behind the bar. The big screen is rolled up into the ceiling for the night. Ravens at Browns is on one of the tube TVs in the corner with the volume down to a mutter, and the touchdown bell over the bar is tied off with a bar towel, the way Sully ties it on nights that haven’t earned it.

Dale is at the end of the bar in the Barry Sanders jersey, which he has worn every Sunday since September as a vigil and has apparently extended to Mondays. Jack has a booth to himself and a Coke he’s been making last since kickoff. A Coke at Sully’s is two-fifty, and the refill policy is between the bartender and his conscience.

Lena comes in at the end of the first quarter in the cardigan, with a root beer in each hand and a holy card pinched under one thumb against the bottle. She puts a root beer in front of him and slides in across the booth and props the card against the ketchup, facing the screen: St. Jude, green cloak, a little flame over his head.
“You watched mine win nine times, Youngstown,” she says. “I owe you a Monday.”

body.text: And then, under the TV, so only he gets it: “And it’s Monday.”

body: Dale cranes down the bar at the card. “That a saint?”
“St. Jude,” Lena says. “Hopeless cases. He’s for causes, Dale, not teams.”

“Young lady, the Lions have had that man on retainer since 1957.” He lifts his beer to the card anyway, and then, as one bereaved man to another, to Jack: “We get you people Sunday. Ford Field. Somebody’s gonna win a football game and it’s gonna be a tragedy either way.”

Jack does the first half as a wake. He gives Brady Quinn’s eulogy at the two-minute warning — a good son of Dublin, Ohio, a credit to Notre Dame, a man who threw the ball with real feeling in the general direction of other men — and he gives it again at the half, longer, because it’s nothing to nothing and the deceased has two quarters left. He does Eric Mangini’s press conference. He does the Dawg Pound as the Book of Lamentations. Lena puts her forehead down on the table twice.

The third quarter takes three minutes. The Ravens put up thirteen points in them, one of the touchdowns Dawan Landry going forty-eight yards the other way with a Quinn pass while the Browns offense watches him go like a bus they missed.
“St. Jude,” Lena says, squinting at the card, “has limits.”
It ends 16–0. Jack reads Quinn’s line off the screen in the voice his father uses for the obituaries: thirteen of thirty-one, ninety-nine yards, two interceptions.

choices.text: Pray to the card anyway. Out loud. For Brady Quinn’s soul.
response: Jack folds his hands over St. Jude and prays to him out loud, perfectly deadpan, at a volume that carries to the pool table: for Brady Quinn, who has suffered; for his offensive line, who were elsewhere; for the city of Cleveland, which has done nothing to deserve this except be Cleveland.
At the end of the bar Dale takes his cap off and holds it over the Barry Sanders jersey. Lena has to put her root beer down.

choices.text: “That’s not a lost cause. That’s a franchise.”
response: “That’s not a lost cause,” Jack says, nodding at the screen. “That’s a franchise.”

Lena slaps the table so hard the saint falls over. Dale says “*Hey*,” like he’s the one who’s been insulted, and then laughs into his beer, and the bartender comes down the bar to stand St. Jude back up against the ketchup himself.

choices.text: “Thanks for coming.”
response: “Thanks for coming,” Jack says.
Lena looks at him over the root beer. “I’m with Julian, Jack,” she says. “I’m not *dead*.” Then she steals a sip of his Coke and makes a face at how flat it’s gone.

s24a.slug: MONDAY · 8:40 PM · MISSION STREET, THE 11 BUS SHELTER
body: The shelter on Mission is a bench, a schedule last updated during the Clinton administration and a fluorescent tube that buzzes like it has something on its mind. Lena sits under it with Hale’s packet open on her knee, running a yellow highlighter down the margin.
The RAZR goes in his pocket. MOM. It’s twenty to twelve on Glenwood Avenue.
“Go,” Lena says, without looking up from the packet.

He walks a block up Mission and round the corner past the laundromat, where the dryers are turning behind the glass over a row of empty plastic chairs, and he stands with his back to the brick and the traffic between him and the shelter, and keeps his voice down anyway.
“*Zero!*” his mother says. “Did you *see*? *Zero.*”
He saw.
Then, with no breath in between, because she’s been sitting on it all game: “So? Christmas? Idaho?”
“Ma —”

“I wrote her already. Last week. On the good notepaper.” The good notepaper is the parish stationery with the crest, kept in the hutch for sympathy cards and First Communions. “A mother can write a girl. She wrote Rosie, didn’t she?”

body.text: “And Gina says the nun’s not coming.”

body: “She’s got a boyfriend, Ma.”
“*Again?*” His mother takes that in. “Madonna. Well. Idaho, then.”
There’s a click, and the hiss of the extension, and somebody breathing on the line. “Zero,” his father says. Click.

Jack listens for where. His mother is moving with the cordless — slippers on the linoleum, the back door — and then, faint and steady under her voice, the space heater in the garage, its fan rattling in its cage the way it has every winter of his life.
“He watched it home,” his mother says. “In the garage.”
Nonna’s asleep in the chair again, she says; still won’t do the stairs. Then she tells him to go to bed, it’s nearly midnight, and he doesn’t tell her it isn’t nearly midnight here.

When he comes back round the corner the 11 is pulling in, and Lena is up at the curb with the packet under her arm. She doesn’t ask. She gets on first and goes down the aisle and takes the aisle seat, and leaves him the window.

s26.slug: WEDNESDAY · 2:05 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE KITCHEN OFF THE FISHBOWL
body: The toaster in the kitchen off the Fishbowl ticks while it heats. Tick, and tick, the coils going orange through the slots, and at five past two in the morning it’s the loudest thing on the ground floor of Delgado. The Mr. Coffee has an inch of something black in it from Monday. The dented Newman stockpot Lena still hasn’t taken back is upside down in the dish rack. On the other side of the glass the Fishbowl is dark, the couches just shapes, and past it the sodium lamp makes an empty orange room out of the Anacapa lawn.

He got in from the Tuesday shift at twenty past one and didn’t go up. He’s making toast because his hands want something to do. The jar is on the counter by the toaster, purple-black, the lid labeled in a mother’s Sharpie: JACK.

It’s two in the morning. On the bleachers in September Becca said she’d pray for two in the morning, and Becca does what she says. Somewhere across the lawn, if he knows her at all, a girl with her grandmother’s rosary has this exact hour in her hands, for him.

The toast comes up. He spreads the jam with the back of a spoon, because the knives are all in the sink, and while he does it he walks her through the house. He can’t stop. He’s been doing it since noon yesterday.

She comes up the porch steps on Glenwood Avenue on the twenty-seventh of December in her Carhartt vest with a suitcase she packed a week early, and the porch is cold the way it’s always cold, and his mother has the door open before she’s up the steps. Rosie’s crab drawings are on the refrigerator under the St. Brigid’s magnet, and Becca can name every crab. Nonna sits her down at the kitchen table and wraps the beads around her hand and teaches her the Hail Mary in Calabrese, and Becca has it the first time, because Becca has everything the first time. His father is out in the garage, so Becca goes out to the garage, and by the second night his father likes her against his will and isn’t going to say so to anybody, ever. Gina rolls her eyes at her the first day and on the third day lets her braid her hair. And at dinner there’s the chair.

Becca would ask about the chair. She’d be gentle; she’s always gentle about a thing like that. His mother would tell her at the sink with her back turned, and Becca would put down the dish towel and take his mother’s hand. And from that night on, for the rest of her life — on the ranch, in a kitchen of her own someday with nine kids at the table and her grandmother’s rosary worn smooth — Becca Lindell would pray for Danny Costigan by name. Every night. She wouldn’t miss one.

They’d love her. Every one of them would love her, and every one of them would believe it. His mother would stand at the stove and hope, right there in front of Nonna, in front of the chair, as hard as she knows how. And Jack would stand in his mother’s kitchen next to a girl he isn’t going to marry, and let her.
He puts the spoon down.

All fall there’s been a reason to wait, and the reason had a name. On Friday, under the eucalyptus, the name went to dinner with somebody else. So there’s nothing to wait for now. There’s nobody. He lifts the reason off, the way you’d lift your hand off a stack of papers by an open window to see what blows — and nothing moves. Not a sheet. Lena is with somebody, there’s nobody left to wait for, and he still can’t take Becca home. It isn’t about Lena. That’s how he knows.
Out past the glass, over the black of the Lagoon, a single falling star goes down the sky, quick and white, and out.

choices.text: Pray for her. By name. At the minute she’s praying for you.
response: He stands at the counter with the toast going cold and prays for her. Not well. A Hail Mary, and then her name, *Becca*, and then *Rebecca*, the way his mother wrote it on the good notepaper, and then just the name, over and over, at the minute she’s praying for him. Somewhere in there the toaster stops ticking. He eats the toast cold, every bite, because her mother made the jam.
At two minutes past seven, from his bed, with Theo still asleep, he types it on the keypad a letter at a time and sends it.

choices.text: The east stairs. The window. A Marlboro.
response: He leaves the toast on the counter and goes up the east stairs to the fourth-floor landing and shoves the window up as far as it will go, and lights a Red off the second match. It tastes the way it always tastes, like an idea he’s already had and knows the end of. He smokes it down to his fingers looking at the dark where the Grove is and not thinking about anything, which takes everything he’s got.
At two minutes past seven, from his bed, with Theo still asleep, he types it on the keypad a letter at a time and sends it.

choices.text: Write it in pencil in Hale’s margin: *I can’t take her home.*
response: He gets Hale’s reader out of his bag and finds a pencil, and in the margin beside a paragraph of Kant on the murderer at the door he writes it in small letters, so it will be true somewhere outside his head: *I can’t take her home.*
Then he looks at it. Gray pencil on cheap copy paper, next to Kant. It doesn’t look like much. It doesn’t have to.
At two minutes past seven, from his bed, with Theo still asleep, he types it on the keypad a letter at a time and sends it.

s28.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:00 PM · PORTOLÁ LOT, THE RANGER
body: The Ranger’s heater ticks. With the doors shut it’s the only sound in the cab besides the engine turning over low under the floor — a small dry tick behind the dash every second or so, keeping time for somebody. Becca has had it running since before he came across the lot. It’s dark at six now. Portolá’s windows are lit in rows over the lot and the lot lights have come on orange over the cars, and none of it gets very far into the cab.

It’s Eli’s truck: the red ’94 with the Idaho plates and the Rathdrum Feed & Seed sticker peeling at one corner of the back glass, a bench seat with a Pendleton blanket over the split in the vinyl, St. Isidore clipped to the visor on her side with his plow. Two coffees in the cupholders, because she’s Becca and it’s six o’clock. His has a J on the lid in her marker. The planner is up on the dash, open to December. On the twenty-seventh, in pencil: PIT?
Her truck. Her heater, her keys, her saint. Whatever gets said in here, she can put it in drive whenever she’s ready, and nobody can make her wait. He’d have picked it himself if she hadn’t.
“They were out of the regular,” she says. “Yours is hazelnut. I’m sorry. I tasted it, it’s fine, it just tastes like a candle.”
He picks it up and holds it and doesn’t drink it. He has nothing funny in him tonight, and he doesn’t go looking.
She looks at his face once, in the orange from the lot. Then she reaches up and closes the planner before he’s said a word, and sets it on her knee with her hand on the cover.
“Is this a bad thing?”

choices.text: “I can’t take you home. It would be a lie, and you’d believe it.”
choices.key: In Eli’s truck you told Becca the truth: you can’t take her home. It would be a lie, and she’d believe it.
response: “I can’t take you home,” Jack says. “It would be a lie, and you’d believe it.”

Becca puts her hands on the wheel. She nods at the dark windshield, slowly — the nod she gives a weather report: no use arguing with it; you dress for it. “Okay,” she says. She keeps hold of the wheel.

choices.text: “You deserve somebody who doesn’t have to try this hard to be in the room with you.”
choices.key: In Eli’s truck you told Becca she deserves somebody who doesn’t have to try that hard.
response: “You deserve somebody,” Jack says, “who doesn’t have to try this hard to be in the room with you.”

Becca puts her hands on the wheel. “Try,” she says, as if she’s found it on the floor of the cab and is turning it over to see what it is. “You were *trying*?” He has nothing to put against it. She nods at the dark windshield, slowly — the nod she gives a weather report.

choices.text: “I’m not right for you, Becca.”
choices.key: In Eli’s truck you told Becca you’re not right for her.
response: “I’m not right for you, Becca.”

“Okay,” Becca says, eventually. She puts her hands on the wheel and nods at the dark windshield, as if that’s a thing a person could know about himself and she ought to respect it. Then, because she’s Becca and she has to check: “Not right how?”

s28a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:14 PM · PORTOLÁ LOT, THE RANGER
body: Becca looks out at the lot. When she says it, it isn’t an accusation. She says it quietly, the way she says the answer to a problem she’s finally gotten, almost relieved to have it.
“You were going to bring *her*.”

She was praying Lena would say yes. She tells him that too. “I really was. Every night. I put it in with two in the morning.” She smooths the planner’s cover with her thumb. “I had it all worked out. She’d be at your mom’s and I’d be at ours, and I’d call during Dad’s grace, and you’d hold the phone out so everybody could hear him do the cows. I thought that was a good plan.” She says it like it was. It was.

body.text: “You said ‘not yet,’ Sunday.” She looks up at the visor. “I knew.”
“You told me Sunday it’s okay.” She picks her coffee up out of the cupholder and puts it back without drinking any. “It wasn’t, though.”

choices.text: “Yes.”
response: “Yes,” Jack says.
Becca nods. She takes it the way she took the first thing, all of it at once, without making him say any more. “Thank you,” she says, “for not saying no.”

choices.text: “She’s with Julian. And I still can’t take you.”
response: “She’s with Julian,” Jack says. “And I still can’t take you.”
It takes her a second. He watches her get there: her eyes go down to the planner on her knee, and her mouth goes small. “Oh,” Becca says. “Oh, Jack. That’s worse. That’s so much worse for *you*.”

choices.text: “This isn’t about Lena.”
response: “This isn’t about Lena,” Jack says.
“Okay,” Becca says, and he can see that she believes him. She always has. She takes her hands off the wheel long enough to wipe her palms down her Wranglers, and puts them back.

s28b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:31 PM · PORTOLÁ LOT, THE RANGER
body: The heater ticks. Out in the lot somebody’s car chirps twice, locking, and a girl in a Portolá sweatshirt crosses behind the truck with a laundry basket on her hip.
Becca is working it out loud, step by step, showing her work. “I did everything right. I know I did. It just isn’t the thing, is it.”
“You did,” Jack says. It’s the one thing in the cab he’s sure of. Past that he has no argument. There isn’t one; he’s looked.
“You looked at me like homework,” she says. “I thought if I was really good homework —” She stops.

Then she cries, with the engine running and her hands on the wheel, without making any noise at all. It’s a farm hand’s grip, knuckles up, marker still on two of them from some poster for Newman, and she holds on through it and looks straight out the windshield at Portolá’s lit windows and lets it come down her face. Jack sits on his side of the bench seat with his hands between his knees and lets her have the cab. There are Arby’s napkins in the door pocket on his side. He finds them and puts them on the seat by her leg, and eventually she takes one and holds it.

After a minute she says, in the voice she uses for procedure, the voice from the beach cleanup and the clipboard: “Can you leave Facebook? Till I’m home? Mom first. Then Facebook. I want to tell her at the table, not on a computer.”
“Okay.”
“Eli’s going to know,” she says. “He always knows when somebody’s cried in his truck. He says it gets in the upholstery.” She folds the napkin into a square on her knee and presses it flat.
“And Theo keeps his jar.” She wipes her nose with the napkin, finally. “It isn’t *his* fault.”

body.text: “Daisy’s money’s still there if you get short for the bus.” A breath. “You can’t take my heifer. I know.”
body.else: “Daisy’s money’s still there if you get short for the bus. That’s a Newman thing, not a girlfriend thing.”

body: Then she reaches across the seat and turns his collar down, the flannel, which has been up on one side since the Anacapa lawn. She’s done it a hundred times. Her hand stops on it halfway, and she takes it back and puts it on the wheel.
“Go on, Jack,” she says. “I’m going to cry in Eli’s truck and you’re in it.”

choices.text: “I’ll pray for you. Every day.”
response: “I’ll pray for you,” he says. “Every day.”
“I know you will.” Becca nods at the windshield. “Me too. I’m not going to stop just because.”
He opens the door, and the cold comes into the cab, and he gets out into it.

choices.text: Get out. Close the door gently.
response: He doesn’t say anything else. He gets out, and he eases the door to, slow, holding the handle out until the latch takes, so it won’t make a sound in there.
Through the glass he sees her put her forehead down on the top of the wheel.

choices.text: “God bless, Becca.”
response: “God bless, Becca.”

“God bless,” she says back — the way everybody says it at Coffee & Donuts at the end of every Sunday, to everybody — and for a second that’s all it is: a Sunday, and the folding tables, and the olive tree. Then he gets out into the cold.

s28c.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:52 PM · PORTOLÁ HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: He gets as far as the Portolá steps and sits down on them in the cold. The Ranger doesn’t move. He can hear it idling across the lot, and nothing else; without the heater ticking in his ear the lot has its own sound, the sodium lamps humming on their poles.

After a minute the dome light comes on in the cab. She’s reached up and switched it on herself, and he can see her small and yellow in it, bent over something on her knee. The planner, maybe. The light stays on a long time. Then, all at once, the dome light goes off.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s closer than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table.

journal.title: Thanksgiving
journal.text: Wes will be at the Broussards’ table on Thanksgiving, like every year since the storm. He carried the twins out of a second floor. Lena says she’d go anywhere nobody knows his name. I’m going to ask her to Youngstown — properly, in a week. Not one breath after Becca’s name. A week to the night, I asked about the table. She’ll be okay. Julian says call him from the bathroom. I didn’t ask the other thing. Becca’s done. It’s me and the Greyhound.

body: At twenty to eleven the fourth-floor lounge has one lamp on, the one with the shade scorched brown on the side everybody keeps turned to the wall, and the window over the couch is black glass with the lamp in it. Jack is on the end of the couch with Hale’s reader open on his knee to a page he hasn’t read.

body.text: Behind him Margot’s whiteboard still says BOTH from last Monday, underlined, against her will.
Behind him Margot’s whiteboard still says COSTIGAN — CANDLES from last Monday.
Behind him Margot’s whiteboard still says BROUSSARD, ON POINTS from last Monday.

body: Lena comes in from the east stairs in her socks, so he doesn’t hear her until she’s in the doorway: the cardigan over flannel pajama pants printed with crawfish, thick gray socks, a Community Coffee mug held up under her chin in both hands.
“Are you okay?”
He thinks about it honestly, and gives her the only answer he’s got. “Ask me again in a week.”

It gets her. She shuts her eyes and shakes her head at him — *no, you don’t get to* — and the laugh comes anyway, short, down her nose, a sound she would clearly like back. She opens her eyes and scowls at him over the mug.
Then she comes the rest of the way in and sits on the other end of the couch with her feet tucked up under her, and holds the mug, and looks at him. “What happened?”

choices.text: “Ma wanted her at Christmas. I couldn’t take her home. I’d have been lying in my mother’s kitchen.”
choices.key: Lena came up in her socks to ask if you were okay. You told her why: you couldn’t take Becca home.
response: “Ma wanted her at Christmas,” Jack says. “I couldn’t take her home. I’d have been lying in my mother’s kitchen.”
At the other end of the couch Lena holds absolutely still, the mug under her chin. Then: “Oh, Jack.”

choices.text: “She didn’t do anything wrong. That’s the whole thing.”
response: “She didn’t do anything wrong,” Jack says. “That’s the whole thing.”
Lena nods into the mug, slowly, like it’s a point she’s conceding.

choices.text: “I don’t want to talk about her. She doesn’t deserve to be talked about.”
response: “I don’t want to talk about her,” Jack says. “She doesn’t deserve to be talked about.”
“Okay,” Lena says, and drops it there.

body: “I’m sorry, Jack,” Lena says. “She’s a good girl.”

And for the next ten minutes she says every right thing there is to say. Has he eaten? He hasn’t, it turns out, since a bagel at eleven. She digs in the cardigan pocket and comes up with half a praline in wax paper, Mémère’s, the pecans showing on the broken side.

body.text: “She says it’s for the boy with manners.”
body.else: “Don’t tell her I gave you one. She counts.”

body: He eats it. It’s so sweet it hurts his back teeth.

“You did the hard thing honest,” she says. “Most people do it on the phone.” Becca will be all right, she tells him — not tonight, but she will; a girl like that has a family and a parish behind her. She’s going to tell Laney to be nice to Becca, starting tomorrow, and Laney is going to do it, because Lena will make her. He should go to the 12:10 tomorrow even if he doesn’t want to. Especially if. She’ll save him the end of a pew. She doesn’t ask about Thanksgiving. Julian doesn’t come up.
Near the end of it he remembers to ask her back. “You okay?”
“Me?” She smiles at him over the mug. “I’m good, Jack. I’m good.”
Her hand goes to the medal at her throat, under the cardigan, and comes back to the mug.

At ten to eleven she unfolds off the couch and tells him to go to sleep, as an order. She sets the mug down on the lounge table to free her hands for the stairwell door, and he watches her go down the long hall toward the east stairs — the cardigan, the crawfish, the gray socks soundless on the linoleum, her fingers trailing along the cinderblock. At the stairwell door she stops with her hand on the bar, long enough that he thinks she’s going to turn around with one more right thing. Then she leans into it and is gone down the stairs.
The mug is still on the lounge table, full to the brim. She never drank any of it. At midnight, when he finally gets up, it’s stone cold, and he picks it up anyway and stands there holding it.
